name: Old English
blurb: The language of Beowulf, King Alfred and Ælfric, and the ancestor of the English you are reading now.
facts: Alfred the Great had Latin books translated into English so that free-born young men could learn to read their own language.
Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, which was scorched in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731.
The letters þ and ƿ (wynn) were borrowed from runes. Early printers wrote þ as y, which is why 'ye olde' really means 'the old'.
Cædmon, a cowherd at Whitby, is the first English poet known by name. Bede tells how he learned to sing in a dream.
Four weekdays keep Old English gods: Tīwesdæg, Wōdnesdæg, Þunresdæg and Frīgedæg belong to Tiw, Woden, Thunor and Frig.

units.title: Fuþorc
units.about: The runes of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc

guide.p: The English rune row is named after its first six letters, f u þ o r c. English and Frisian carvers added new runes as their vowels changed, growing the old 24-rune row to 28 and later to as many as 33.
Every rune has a name that starts with its sound. The Old English Rune Poem gives each one a short verse: feoh 'wealth', ūr 'aurochs', þorn 'thorn'.
The old a-rune split three ways: ᚩ ōs became o, while new runes ᚪ āc and ᚫ æsc took over a and æ. ᚣ ȳr and ᛠ ēar were added later still.
The whalebone Franks Casket is carved with a riddling verse that ends hronæs ban, 'whale's bone'. The Thames scramasax spells out the whole row next to its owner's name.
Scribes writing English in the Latin alphabet kept two runes as letters: þ from þorn and ƿ, wynn, for w.

items.note: The Rune Poem may read it as Latin os, 'mouth'.
The Rune Poem describes a guiding star. The older name meant the god Tiw.

units.title: Hāl wes þū
units.about: Greet people and say who you are

guide.p: Old English has no indefinite article. mann is 'man' or 'a man'.
ic eom 'I am', þū eart 'you are', hē is 'he is', hēo is 'she is'.
hātte means 'am called' or 'is called': ic hātte, hēo hātte. Several Exeter Book riddles end with a dare, saga hwæt ic hātte, 'say what I am called'.
hāl means 'whole, healthy'. hāl wes þū, 'be healthy', is how the Gospels greet a king. To several people: hāle wese gē. Beowulf greets the Danish king with wæs þū, Hrōðgār, hāl.
þ and ð both stand for th. æ is the a of 'cat', and a line over a vowel (ā) marks it long. sc sounds like sh, and c before i or e is often ch, as in cild 'child'.

items.note: Greet someone with hāl wes þū, 'be healthy'.
Means 'person' as well as 'man'. A male is a wer.

guide.p: Every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and 'the' follows suit: se for masculine, sēo for feminine, þæt for neuter.
Gender belongs to the word, not the thing. wīf 'woman' is neuter, so it is þæt wīf.
ne goes before the verb, and ne is fuses into nis, 'is not'.
ex: the father is not at home

guide.p: For a yes-or-no question, put the verb first.

sentences.en: the father is not at home
she is a daughter and a sister

units.title: Meduheall
units.about: King, lord, mead and the object case

guide.p: When a noun is the object of a verb, 'the' changes: se becomes þone and sēo becomes þā. þæt stays the same. Most nouns keep their own form.
Because the article shows who does what, the words can move. þā cwēn lufaþ se cyning still means 'the king loves the queen'. In a main clause the verb usually comes second, as in German.
Weak verbs like lufian 'love' keep their vowel: ic lufie, þū lufast, hē lufaþ.
Strong verbs like drincan 'drink' and singan 'sing' change their vowel in the past (dranc, 'drank'). In the present they take -e, -st, -þ: ic drince, þū drincst, hē drincþ.
on healle is 'in the hall'. The hlāford, 'lord', was once the hlāf-weard, 'loaf-keeper': he shares food and treasure in the hall, and his þegnas repay him with loyalty.

items.note: Feminine. 'In the hall' is on healle.

units.title: Middangeard
units.about: Heaven, earth and the two verbs 'to be'

guide.p: eom, eart, is describe how things are now. bēon, with ic bēo, þū bist, hē biþ, states what is always true and what will be.
The plural of is is sindon: wē sindon, gē sindon, hīe sindon. mann has the plural menn, just like man and men.
Pronouns have object forms: ic becomes mē, þū becomes þē, hē becomes hine, wē becomes ūs.
Nouns ending in -a or -e, like sunne and eorþe, end in -an everywhere except as the subject: sēo eorþe, but on eorþan 'on earth'.
God has a short o, gōd 'good' a long one. middangeard, 'the middle enclosure', is the world of men between heaven and hell, the word Tolkien made into Middle-earth.

items.note: Christian poets use it for God, 'the Lord'.
From bēon. Used for general truths and the future.

units.title: Wyrd
units.about: Proverbs and famous lines of verse

guide.p: sceal means 'must, has to, is bound to'. It takes a plain infinitive ending in -an. The Cotton Maxims open with a list of what each thing should do.
ex: a king must rule a kingdom

guide.p: wyrd is fate, 'what comes to pass'. The Maxims say wyrd biþ swīþost, The Wanderer wyrd biþ ful ārǣd, 'fate is wholly fixed'. Beowulf shrugs: gǣþ ā wyrd swā hīo scel, 'fate always goes as it must'. Manuscripts spell biþ as bið or byð.

-ra means '-er' and -ost '-est'. þē before a comparative means 'all the', and þē also joins clauses as 'as'. The old retainer in The Battle of Maldon (991) rallies the last men around their dead lord with these lines.

Deor ends every stanza with a refrain of comfort: þæs oferēode, þisses swā mæg, 'that passed over, so can this'. The Advent lyric Christ I hails Ēarendel, a morning star, the name Tolkien borrowed for his mariner Eärendil.

items.note: Beowulf opens with it, as a call to listen.

units.title: Gēardagas
units.about: Tell what happened: the past tense

guide.h: Two ways to make a past
guide.p: Weak verbs add -de or -ode: lufian 'love' becomes lufode 'loved', hīeran 'hear' becomes hīerde 'heard'. Strong verbs change their vowel instead, the way English sing becomes sang.
ic and hē share one form: ic sang, hē sang; ic lufode, hē lufode. Every plural subject takes -on: wē sungon, hīe lufodon. þū takes -est in weak verbs (þū lufodest) and -e in strong ones (þū sunge).

Many strong verbs have one vowel for the singular past and another for the plural: hē sang but hīe sungon, hē dranc but hīe druncon. Dictionaries give four forms, singan, sang, sungon, sungen, so that you can find every one.
wesan 'to be' is strong too: ic wæs, þū wǣre, hē wæs, wē wǣron. hæfde 'had' is the past of habban 'have'.
English still has a few dozen strong verbs: drink, drank, drunk and ride, rode, ridden. Many others went weak over the centuries. Old English healp, 'helped', is one of them.

items.note: Past of wesan 'to be'. Plural: wǣron.
From faran 'go, travel', our 'fare'. Plural: fōron.

units.title: Ofer sǣ
units.about: Ships, gifts and the cases for 'of' and 'to'

guide.p: Nouns have four main cases. The nominative is the subject and the accusative the object. The genitive means 'of' or ''s'. The dative means 'to' or 'for', and most prepositions take it.
Most masculine and neuter nouns add -es, which lives on as English 's. 'The' becomes þæs, or þǣre with a feminine noun, which usually ends in -e: þǣre cwēne 'the queen's'.
The dative marks the one something is given or said to. Masculine and neuter nouns add -e, and 'the' becomes þǣm (also spelled þām), or þǣre with a feminine noun.
ex: se cyning geaf þǣm þegne bēag
the king gave the thane a ring

guide.p: tō 'to', mid 'with', of 'out of' and fram 'from' take the dative. on, in, ofer and under take the dative for where something is and the accusative for where it is going. on healle 'in the hall' was a dative all along.
In the plural 'the' is þā, 'of the' is þāra and 'to the' is þǣm. Masculine nouns like bēag add -as, bēagas 'rings', and every dative plural ends in -um.
The Beowulf poet calls a king bēaga brytta, 'giver of rings'. A lord handed out arm-rings and gold in his hall, and the gift bound the warrior to him.

items.note: Dative of se and þæt. Also spelled þām. Feminine: þǣre.
Genitive of se and þæt. Feminine: þǣre.
A gold arm-ring, the classic gift of a lord.
Its dative is also sǣ: on sǣ 'at sea'.

units.title: Wit and git
units.about: Every pronoun, including 'we two' and 'you two'

guide.p: Pronouns have four cases, like nouns. The dative means 'to me, to him': mē, þē, him, hire, ūs. The genitive means 'of me' and doubles as 'my': mīn, þīn, his, hire, ūre.

Old English kept a dual for pairs: wit 'we two' and git 'you two', with unc 'us two' and inc 'you two' as objects. Beowulf recalls a boyhood swimming match with wit þæt gecwǣdon, 'we two agreed on that'.

The speaker of The Wife's Lament remembers how ful oft wit bēotedan, 'very often we two vowed', that only death would part them. Wulf and Eadwacer ends with uncer giedd geador, 'the song of us two together'.
mīn, þīn, ūre and ēower 'your (plural)' take adjective endings, so 'my' changes with its noun: mīn fæder, but mīnne fæder as an object. his, hire and hiera 'their' never change.
þū is one person and gē is several, the 'thou' and 'ye' of older English. hīe means 'they', and also 'her' as an object. The th- of 'they' arrived later, from Old Norse.

items.note: Object form of wit. For git: inc.
'Her' as in 'her ring' and 'to her'. As an object: hīe.
Dative of hē and hit, and also of hīe 'they'.

units.title: Canst þū singan?
units.about: Can, may, must and want: the modal verbs

guide.p: sculan 'must', willan 'want', magan 'be able', mōtan 'be allowed' and cunnan 'know how' take a plain infinitive in -an, just as sceal did in the Maxims. The infinitive usually comes late in the clause.

These verbs have no -þ for hē: ic mæg, hē mæg, þū meaht; ic sceal, þū scealt; ic cann, þū canst; ic mōt, þū mōst. Plurals end in -on: wē magon, wē sculon, wē cunnon. willan goes ic wille, þū wilt, hē wile.
Their pasts are weak: sceolde 'had to', wolde 'wanted', meahte 'could', mōste 'was allowed', cūþe 'knew how'. They became should, would, might and must, and cūþe became could.
mōtan means 'may, be allowed to' far more often than 'must'. cunnan means 'know', as in uncouth, from uncūþ 'unknown'. helpan takes a dative: helpan þǣm cyninge 'help the king'.
In the Old English Bede, a figure in a dream tells Cædmon to sing. He answers ne con ic nōht singan, 'I cannot sing anything'. Told hwæðre þū meaht singan, 'yet you can sing', he asks what to sing.

items.note: From cunnan. þū canst, wē cunnon.
Past of magan. Also spelled mihte.

units.title: Eald and geong
units.about: Strong and weak adjectives, and comparison

guide.p: After se, sēo, þæt or mīn, an adjective takes weak endings: -a for a masculine subject, -e for a feminine or neuter one, and -an almost everywhere else.

With no article, adjectives take strong endings that echo the article: gōdne like þone, gōdes like þæs, gōdre like þǣre. After is, an adjective usually has no ending at all. The Beowulf poet praises Scyld with þæt wæs gōd cyning.
ex: he gave me a good ring

guide.p: -ra makes '-er' and -ost or -est makes '-est'. Comparatives always take weak endings, so a queen is wīsre, 'wiser'. þonne means 'than'.

Some adjectives change their vowel as well: eald, ieldra, ieldest 'old, older, oldest' and lang, lengra, lengest, the same change as long and length. A few switch words: gōd, betera, betst; micel, māra, mǣst; lȳtel, lǣssa, lǣst.

When Beowulf's men desert him, Wiglaf tells them dēaþ biþ sēlla eorla gehwylcum þonne edwītlīf. sēlla is a second word for 'better', and eorla gehwylcum, 'for each of warriors', means 'for every warrior'.

items.note: Comparative of gōd. sēlra means the same.

guide.p: A line of Old English verse is two half-lines with a pause between them. Each half has two stressed syllables, and the unstressed ones can vary in number. Editions print a gap at the pause.
ex: Beowulf 4: three of the four beats begin with sc

guide.p: The halves are bound by sound, not rhyme. The first stress of the second half sets the sound, and one or both stresses of the first half must match it. The last stress in the line does not alliterate.
ex: he grew under the skies, prospered in honours (Beowulf 8)

guide.p: Any vowel alliterates with any other vowel. sc, sp and st match only themselves. The two sounds of g count as one, so Gār-Dena alliterates with gēardagum in the first line of Beowulf.

A kenning names a thing through a picture: the sea is the hronrād 'whale-road', the body a bānhūs 'bone-house', the sun the woruldcandel 'world-candle'. Some are phrases, such as goldwine gumena, 'gold-friend of men', for a king.
Poets name one thing several ways in a row. Cædmon calls God heofonrīces weard, wuldorfæder, ēce drihten and hālig scyppend in nine lines. In The Wanderer, cwōm is an old spelling of cōm 'came'.

items.note: A kenning for a sword in Beowulf 1143, and for fire in 2583.
